title: Sprocket and the Lost Glow-Bug
markdown:
Prayer flags snapped between the teeth of the High Valley Archipelago. Fir branches took the mist and gave it back as bells. Sprocket’s house hung on a cliff the way a stubborn idea hangs on a person. Usually the wind was company. Today it only kept time with the fuss in his ribs.

“Flicker,” he said, not quite a shout. “The festival is almost here.”

Flicker was a firefly with a talent for invention and a worse talent for timing. His light could make a bored pixie reconsider boredom. He was also, at present, missing. The Mist Blossom Festival began at sundown. The Grand Luminary Competition sat in the middle of it like a jewel someone had dared Sprocket to reach. Flicker had taken his glow and gone.

Rook, the raven on Sprocket’s shoulder, offered a croak that years had translated: check the inconvenient place first.

“That is exactly where he would be.” Sprocket settled his goggles. Flicker collected heights, ledges, and other people’s architecture. The oldest monastery’s belfry was not impossible. Reaching it meant a rope ferry that looked knitted by a nervous spider.

They started lower, at the foothills bakery, which smelled of cinnamon and dough that knew its own mind. Bartholomew Buttercrumb filled the doorway. Barty’s oven was clockwork and vain about it; every stage of baking had a chime, and Barty arranged his life around those chimes as if they were tides.

Sprocket stepped over a flour drift. “Have you seen Flicker? The festival is rather important.”

Barty paused with a gingerbread mountain under his duster. The oven ticked, a deep agreeable tick. “Timing is everything. Find what is lost where it is most illuminating.” He went back to the peak as if the sentence had been a completed loaf.

Sprocket turned the word illuminating over and found no handles. Rook’s caw suggested Barty had been as useful as a cloud in a drought.

The Festival Committee heard him thinking and, being a committee of gnomes and pixies, promoted the thought to policy. Sprocket had muttered that Flicker needed a really good spotlight. Crystal began rising in the square, a beacon tower aimed at the next valley. He had sighed that the search felt gloomy. Orders went out for a hundred thousand fireflies to be caught and released at once, a blinking weather system with no forecast.

“If you are going to be mysterious,” Sprocket told Rook, while pixies hurried past with a magnifying glass large enough to insult the sun, “you could at least be on time. They have turned a missing friend into a circus, and I appear to be the clown.”

They climbed. The goat path tried to resign. A shadow passed that was not weather. A dragon turned above them, copper and emerald, and dipped a wing. The gust that followed flattened hair and manners. It also snapped a prayer flag into a panic and, more usefully, shouldered open a crevice Sprocket had walked past without seeing. From the dark mouth came a pulse of light, on, off, on, like a shy hello.

“Flicker.”

The dragon hummed, a note Sprocket felt in his teeth, and left them the wind.

He squeezed through. Rook followed, complaining in the register of ravens who dislike ceilings. Inside, rare moss made its own lamps. Flicker sat in the middle of that borrowed shine and flashed an apology in a dialect of blinks. The moss took his glow and made a room of it. Barty’s word fitted at last: illuminating, not as a riddle, as a place. Flicker had found a spotlight that grew on stone.

The committee, unfortunately, had not vanished. On the way down the crystal tower stood half-finished and very sure of itself. Gnomes herded captured fireflies that had unionised around the idea of escape. Sprocket cupped Flicker and found a voice that did not squeak.

“I have him,” he said. “And the competition has been slightly misread.”

He showed them what Flicker actually did: colour shifting, a dimming, a brightening, patterns like starlight that had learned manners. He told them the moss was already a better stage than any polished spike. The committee, which loved a spectacle and was not immune to a prettier one, watched until their plans looked suddenly heavy.

They turned the tower into a stand for smaller sculptures. The captured fireflies went back to being weather. On the horizon the sun sat down. Barty’s oven chimed as if it had been consulting the same sky, and the ogre arrived with a cart of pastries that had been timed to the minute. The smell made the square remember it was a festival and not an emergency.

Flicker rode Sprocket’s finger and kept a warm, unshowy light over the grove. Rook preened, which was his version of a report. The archipelago bells found one another across the mist. Sprocket did not announce a moral. He watched the last of the herded glow join the real dusk, and he kept his hand cupped a moment longer than he needed, in case the firefly got another idea.
characters: Sprocket (goblin whose home clings to a cliff), Rook (a raven who croaks inconvenient truths), Bartholomew Buttercrumb (an ogre baker with impeccable timing)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for teens
author: StoryGen Community
